family.name: Trooper
family.verdict: Isuzu drew a box, sold it under about a dozen badges on four continents, then spent four years in court defending its honour. The first one is a tall, honest tool; the second is a roomy V6 cruiser with a solid rear axle and a thirst for oil.
intro: Isuzu built the Trooper from September 1981 to September 2002, across two generations. It started life as a wagon on the company's pickup chassis and grew into a full-size, V6-powered family 4x4. Japan knew it as the Bighorn, and the rest of the world met it under other names: Holden Jackaroo and Monterey in Australia, Opel and Vauxhall Monterey in Europe, Honda Horizon in Japan, Acura SLX in the US, plus Chevrolet Trooper and Subaru Bighorn. SsangYong even built it under licence with its own bodywork, as the Korando Family.

The [[trooper/trooper-1|first generation]] (1981–1991) is the boxiest: a narrow, upright wagon with independent torsion-bar front suspension, leaf springs at the back and four-cylinder engines, sold in the US from 1984 as the Trooper II. The [[trooper/trooper-2|second generation]] (1991–2002) added Isuzu's aluminium 3.2- and 3.5-liter V6s, coil springs at the back and, from 1998, Torque On Demand. It won its class in the 1994 Paris–Dakar and won the Australian Safari again and again as the Holden Jackaroo.

In America the second generation is also remembered for a fight. Consumer Reports rated the 1995–96 Trooper and Acura SLX 'Not Acceptable' for rollover risk in 1996. NHTSA declined to open a defect investigation, Isuzu sued, and in 2000 a jury found some of the magazine's statements false but awarded no damages. Today both generations are cheap, capable boxes. Buy a first-generation truck for its simplicity and check it for rust; buy a second-generation one for space and towing, and check the oil.

page.title: Isuzu Trooper (first generation)
page.verdict: A pickup truck wearing a shoebox, and that's a compliment. The first Trooper is narrow, tall, slow and gloriously honest, with more cargo room than it has any right to. Buy the rust-free one, not the shiny one.

paragraphs: In September 1981 Isuzu announced a compact four-wheel-drive wagon called the Rodeo Bighorn. Underneath it was the company's own pickup, sold in America as the Isuzu P'UP and Chevy LUV. Car and Driver reckoned that almost everything under the squarish steel skin, from the chassis to the driveline, was identical or very similar to the four-wheel-drive pickup. On top sat a body drawn with a set square: flat glass, flat sides and a roof you could land a helicopter on. It would be sold under more names than almost any SUV in history, and every one of them was a box.

story.heading: THE TROOPER II ARRIVES
paragraphs: America got it for 1984 as the Trooper II, a two-door imported as a truck. Isuzu chose to pay the 25 percent duty on light trucks rather than squeeze it into Japan's car import quotas, which is why the rear seat was a $300 option. The 'II' marked that truck version; a passenger-car 'Trooper I' was promised and never came. Car and Driver's May 1984 test car had the 1.95-liter four with 82 hp, a four-speed manual and a 13.2-gallon tank. The magazine called the power modest and the ride about as plush as a 4x4 got, and estimated the base price at well under $9,000.

Isuzu's own 1985 brochure shows how quickly the truck grew. That year brought a four-door body, a 2.3-liter gas four, a 2.2-liter turbo-diesel (not sold in California), a five-speed, auto-locking front hubs, three skid plates and a 21.9-gallon tank. The brochure also boasted that the Trooper II had been named 4-Wheel & Off-Road magazine's 1985 '4x4 of the Year', ahead of rivals including the [[jeep/cherokee-xj|Jeep Cherokee]] and Toyota 4Runner.

story.heading: GROWING UP, 1987–1991
paragraphs: For 1987 the Trooper II got flush rectangular headlights, a bold new grille, a wider track and bigger P235/75R15 tires, and the four-door could now be had as a plusher LS. The brochure quoted 96 hp and 123 lb-ft from the 2.3-liter four, and the same brochure shows a Trooper II racing in the Baja 1000's Class 14 in November 1986. For 1988 the 2.6-liter 4ZE1 with fuel injection and 120 hp arrived, and for 1989 Isuzu added an optional 2.8-liter General Motors V6, the pushrod engine from the Chevrolet S-10, until its own V6 was ready.

Late trucks could also be had with a four-speed automatic: Wikipedia says four-cylinder trucks used an Aisin A340H and V6 trucks a GM 4L30E. The basic hardware never changed much. An independent front end on torsion bars, a live rear axle on leaf springs, part-time four-wheel drive and a two-speed transfer case made it more capable than its skinny tires and narrow track suggested. In 1989 only, Isuzu sent America the short-wheelbase, two-door Trooper RS (see the sidebar).

story.heading: ONE BOX, MANY BADGES
paragraphs: Outside the US the truck was everywhere, under different names. Australians and New Zealanders bought it as the Holden Jackaroo, named after the word for a young man working on a sheep or cattle station. Indonesia and South America knew it as the Chevrolet Trooper, Venezuela built it locally as the Caribe 442, and in Japan it was the Isuzu Bighorn. From November 1988 Subaru sold a Bighorn of its own, only with Irmscher trim and the 2.8-liter turbo-diesel. Isuzu also offered a limited run of 100 Bighorn Irmscher R models, with Recaro seats and graphics but no extra power.

The strangest relative came from Korea. In November 1988 SsangYong began licensed production of the Trooper under its own bodywork as the Korando Family, first with the Trooper's 2.2-liter diesel and later with Peugeot and Mercedes-Benz diesels. Rival boxes of the era included the [[pajero/pajero-gen1|first Mitsubishi Pajero]] and Toyota's [[4runner/1st-gen|4Runner]], while Curbside Classic's owner story compares the Trooper's shape to the [[range-rover/classic|Range Rover]] at less than half the price.

story.heading: HOW IT ENDED
paragraphs: Isuzu replaced it with a bigger, more luxurious [[trooper/trooper-2|second-generation Trooper]] in December 1991. The old shape went out on a high in Australia, where a short-wheelbase Holden Jackaroo won the Marathon class of the 1989 Australian Safari in Peter Lockhart's hands, and it lived on for years in Korea as the Korando Family.

Today the first Trooper is a cult truck with modest prices: Bring a Trailer sales from 2024 to 2026 run from $3,500 for a 2.6-powered 1986 project to $14,250 for a 1986 two-door LS five-speed, with a Japanese Bighorn Irmscher at $25,000. Owners love the space and the visibility. They also warn about rusted rear-door hinges, cracked cylinder heads and failed head gaskets on the fours, and wheel studs that strip at the first impact gun. Parts support has thinned, so many owners rely on the Planet Isuzoo community for help.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · THE SHORT ONE
callout.title: Trooper RS and the Safari-winning Jackaroo
paragraphs: For 1989 only, Isuzu imported a short-wheelbase two-door to the US as the Trooper RS. Wikipedia lists the wheelbase at about 90 inches, against 104 for the regular truck. Every RS had the fuel-injected 2.6-liter four, 4.77:1 axle gears and 15 x 7-inch 'snowflake' alloys, with a choice of manual or automatic.
Australia had the same short body as the Jackaroo SWB, and one of them gave the box its best sporting moment of the decade: Peter Lockhart won the Marathon class of the 1989 Australian Safari in one.

page.engineering_intro: The first Trooper is a pickup-derived ladder frame with an independent, torsion-bar front end and a leaf-sprung live rear axle. Four-wheel drive is part-time, through a two-speed transfer case and either auto-locking or manual front hubs. Engines started as small Isuzu fours and finished with a GM V6, and the wheels bolt on with six studs on a 139.7 mm circle.

buying_checks.head: Rust first, everything else second
buying_checks.body: Check the rear cargo doors, their hinges and pins, the floors and the sills. Isuzu recalled 1984–87 trucks (92V093) because salt-belt corrosion in the rear-door hinges could let the doors close in a false latch, and a Curbside Classic reader summed up the rest: once the rear doors started to rust, it was game over.

buying_checks.head: Look at every wheel stud
buying_checks.body: Stripped or snapped wheel studs and galled lug nuts are among the most common owner complaints logged with NHTSA for 1988–91 Troopers, and Curbside Classic's owner broke them too. Make sure all 24 studs are present and the nuts thread on by hand.

buying_checks.head: Ask about the head and head gasket
buying_checks.body: NHTSA's complaint files for 1988 and 1989 Troopers include several cracked cylinder heads and repeated head-gasket failures, and a Curbside Classic reader lost his truck to 'the head gasket issue'. Look for a history of overheating, coolant in the oil and a radiator that hasn't been neglected.

buying_checks.head: Check that the recall work was done
buying_checks.body: 1990–91 trucks were recalled for an oil-cooler hose that could touch the exhaust manifold and melt (90V166), and for automatic transmissions that could spill overfilled fluid onto the exhaust (90V167). On 1987–88 trucks (89V001), a heater bolt could rub through a fuel pipe. NHTSA's 1990–91 complaint files also include several under-hood fires.

buying_checks.head: Engage the hubs and the low range
buying_checks.body: Put it in 4WD high and low on loose ground. Auto-locking hubs should lock and unlock reliably, and the transfer case should shift without a fight. Many owners swap tired auto hubs for manual ones.

buying_checks.head: Know which engine you're getting
buying_checks.body: Early 1.95s and 2.3s are slow; the injected 2.6-liter four (1988–91) and the 2.8-liter GM V6 (1989–91) are the ones to want. US turbo-diesels from the mid-1980s are rare and were never sold in California.

buying_checks.head: Drive the automatic hard
buying_checks.body: A Curbside Classic reader's automatic failed at about 175,000 miles, and NHTSA's 1990–91 complaint files include several slipping, leaking or failed transmissions. A five-speed is the simpler buy.

buying_checks.head: Ask for the timing-belt receipt
buying_checks.body: The Isuzu four-cylinder petrol engines use a timing belt (the 2.3 switched from a chain to a Kevlar belt), so a truck with no record needs one before it goes anywhere remote.

repairs.title: Replace stripped or broken wheel studs
repairs.symptoms: Lug nuts that won't thread on, studs that snap when a tire shop uses an impact gun, or a wheel that loosens. Owners have reported all three to NHTSA.
repairs.fix: Support the truck safely and pull the wheel. On the front, remove the caliper and rotor to reach the back of the hub; on the rear, pull the drum. Drive out the damaged stud, clean the hub, then draw the new stud in with a stack of washers and a lug nut, or press it in, until the head seats fully. Fit new lug nuts with any damaged studs, start every nut by hand and torque them to the factory spec in a star pattern. Tell your tire shop to do the same.
repairs.tools: Hammer and punch or a stud press · washers · torque wrench · factory torque spec [CONFIRM IN MANUAL].

repairs.title: Timing belt on the 2.3 and 2.6 fours
repairs.symptoms: None until it fails. A truck without a belt receipt is due.
repairs.fix: Disconnect the battery, drain the coolant and remove the fan, drive belts and crankshaft pulley, then the timing covers. Set the engine to top dead center and line up the cam and crank timing marks before you loosen anything. Fit the new belt and tensioner, check the marks again after turning the engine over twice by hand, and replace the cam and crank seals if they're weeping. Many owners do the water pump at the same time.
repairs.tools: Socket set · crank-pulley holding tool · torque wrench · factory service manual.

parts.name: Timing belt and component kit, 1990 Trooper 2.6

repairs.title: Cooling-system refresh to protect the head
repairs.symptoms: Creeping temperature, steam, coolant loss or a sweet smell. NHTSA complaint files describe cracked heads and blown head gaskets on 1988–89 trucks.
repairs.fix: With the engine cold, drain the radiator and replace the thermostat, the radiator hoses and the cap. Inspect the radiator for blocked or weeping cores and replace it if in doubt. Refill slowly with the heater on and bleed out air pockets: one 1988 owner blamed air pockets in the head for coolant reaching the cylinders. If the oil looks milky or the cooling system pressurizes quickly, pressure-test it and do a compression or leak-down test before deciding on head work.
repairs.tools: Drain pan · pliers · cooling-system pressure tester · funnel · the coolant type specified for your engine [CONFIRM IN MANUAL].

repairs.title: Service or replace the front locking hubs
repairs.symptoms: Hubs that won't lock in 4WD, grind or clunk when they engage, or won't release.
repairs.fix: Jack up one front wheel at a time. Remove the hub cover bolts and pull the hub body, then clean out old grease and water, check the internals for wear and broken parts and regrease lightly. While it's open, check the wheel-bearing preload and the axle shaft splines. If an auto hub is worn out, many owners fit a pair of manual hubs. Test 4WD high and low on loose ground afterwards.
repairs.tools: Hex keys or sockets · snap-ring pliers · grease · factory manual for bearing preload.

repairs.title: Front CV boots and axles
repairs.symptoms: Grease flung around the inside of the wheel, or a click on full lock under power.
repairs.fix: Support the truck, pull the wheel and the hub, disconnect the lower ball joint or knuckle as the manual describes, and slide the axle out of the differential. Either rebuild the joint with a new boot, clamps and grease, or fit a complete replacement axle. Check the differential output seal while the axle is out.
repairs.tools: Socket set · ball-joint separator · boot-clamp pliers · new axle nut.

repairs.title: Free up and protect the rear-door hinges
repairs.symptoms: Rear doors that sag, bind or don't latch properly. Isuzu's 1992 recall (92V093) covered 1984–87 trucks for exactly this in salt-belt states.
repairs.fix: Support each door before you work on it. Soak the hinge pins with penetrating oil, work them free, clean the knuckles and grease them. Treat rust around the hinge mounts and the bottom of the door shells. Then adjust the latch strikers so each door closes positively, with no false latch.
repairs.tools: Penetrating oil · brass drift · grease · rust converter and paint · screwdrivers for striker adjustment.

repairs.title: Automatic transmission service (and the 90V167 recall check)
repairs.symptoms: Late or harsh shifts, a fluid smell or smoke from the exhaust manifold. On 1990–91 automatics, overfilled fluid could escape onto the exhaust (recall 90V167).
repairs.fix: Drop the pan, replace the filter and gasket, and refill with the specified fluid. Check the level exactly as the manual describes and do not overfill. Confirm with an Isuzu or Chevrolet dealer, or the NHTSA VIN lookup, that the recall work was done.
repairs.tools: Drain pan · socket set · torque wrench · funnel · Dexron-III-type ATF (Liqui Moly lookup; it lists ≈4.5 L for the 1990–92 2.6 automatic).

baseline_service.intro: Treat any first-generation Trooper as unserviced until receipts prove otherwise. These trucks are 35 to 40 years old, so the cheap fluids and rubber parts are what keep the engine and drivetrain alive. Isuzu's factory specs aren't widely published online. The fluid types and capacities below come from Liqui Moly's lookup, which uses European-market Isuzu data, so confirm viscosities and US figures in the owner's or service manual for your engine.

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: The factory size from 1987 was P235/75R15, about 29 inches, on 6.0- or 6.5-inch-wide 15-inch wheels. We couldn't verify a first-generation forum consensus for the largest no-lift size, so check the tire-fitment chart and build threads on Planet Isuzoo before you buy, and check the rear-door-mounted spare carrier too. Wheels are 6 x 139.7 mm with a 100 mm center bore and M12 x 1.5 studs.

faq.q: Why is it called the Trooper II?
faq.a: American Isuzu's product-development manager told Car and Driver in 1984 that 'II' marked the truck version, with the rear seat a $300 option, and 'I' would have been the car version with a standard rear seat. A Trooper I never came. Isuzu imported it as a truck to avoid Japan's car import quotas, and paid the 25 percent truck duty instead.

faq.q: Which engine should I look for?
faq.a: The 1988–91 2.6-liter 4ZE1 is fuel-injected and makes 120 hp; the optional 1989–91 2.8-liter GM V6 makes 122 hp with more torque. The 1984 1.95-liter made 82 hp and the 1985–87 2.3-liter about 96 hp, so early trucks are slow.
faq.src: WIKIPEDIA · CAR AND DRIVER · ISUZU BROCHURE

faq.q: Was there a diesel in the US?
faq.a: Yes. 1984 trucks could have a 2.2-liter pushrod diesel with 62 hp, and from 1985 Isuzu offered a 2.2-liter turbo-diesel (80 hp in the 1987 brochure), which wasn't sold in California. They're rare now; Bring a Trailer sold a 1986 turbo-diesel five-speed for $8,200 in November 2025.
faq.src: CAR AND DRIVER · ISUZU BROCHURES · BAT

faq.q: How does the four-wheel drive work?
faq.a: It's part-time with a two-speed transfer case on its own lever. From 1985 Isuzu fitted auto-locking front hubs, so once they're engaged you can shift between 2WD and 4WD without stopping. Some trucks had Aisin manual hubs instead. Don't drive in 4WD on dry pavement.

faq.q: What fuel economy should I expect?
faq.a: The 1984 1.95-liter was rated at 21 mpg city and 27 highway, and Car and Driver averaged 21 mpg. Isuzu's 1987 brochure lists 17 city and 20 highway for the 2.3-liter five-speed and claims up to 438 miles per tank of gas.

Car and Driver's 1984 two-door had a 1,222 lb payload rating. Isuzu's 1987 brochure lists 1,374 lb (two-door) and 1,319 lb (four-door) for gas trucks, and 79 cubic feet of cargo space with the rear seat removed.

faq.q: How big is the fuel tank?
faq.a: The 1984 truck Car and Driver tested had a 13.2-gallon tank. From 1985 Isuzu quoted 21.9 gallons.

faq.q: Is a Holden Jackaroo or Isuzu Bighorn the same truck?
faq.a: Yes. The Jackaroo (Australia and New Zealand), Bighorn (Japan), Subaru Bighorn, Chevrolet Trooper and Venezuela's Caribe 442 are all the same UBS truck. SsangYong's Korando Family was built under licence with its own bodywork. Imports of Japanese and Australian versions can bring diesel engines the US never got.

Bring a Trailer sales from late 2024 to mid-2026 ranged from $3,500 (a 2.6-powered 1986) to $14,250 (a 1986 Trooper II LS two-door five-speed), with most clean drivers between $7,000 and $9,500. A 1991 Bighorn Irmscher turbo-diesel sold for $25,000 in August 2025.

Service parts such as filters, belts, hubs, CV axles and brake parts are still listed for 1988–91 Troopers at RockAuto. Trim and body parts are harder. Owners on Overland Bound say parts support for Isuzu light trucks has gone downhill, and point to Planet Isuzoo for help.

mods.why: Torsion bars, leaf springs and shocks are 35 years old. Fresh parts restore ride height before you add bigger tires. An Overland Bound member who has owned a first-generation truck calls Independent4x the most readily available source for many Trooper build parts.
Belts, hoses, hubs, CV axles, brakes and ignition parts for the 2.6 and the V6.
The 6 x 139.7 mm bolt pattern, with a 100 mm center bore and M12 x 1.5 studs, opens up a wide choice of wheels. Mind the offset: the factory 15 x 6.5 wheel is listed at +3 mm.
Tire-fitment charts, hub swaps, engine swaps and parts sourcing live on the Planet Isuzoo forums.
